newsitem.title: USA: Georgia bond advisers' libel suit goes to trial.
newsitem.headline: Georgia bond advisers' libel suit goes to trial.

text.p: Atlanta Mayor Bill Campbell testified in a Georgia libel trial that he was ultimately responsible for glitches that forced the city to cancel a 1994 bond referendum.
"He said he was the captain of the ship," attorney Peter Canfield said. He represents Cox Enterprise Inc, the owner of the Atlanta Journal-Constitution.

Bond lawyer Ray Sales and financial adviser William Clement Jr sued the newspaper, alleging it libeled them in a March 10, 1994, story that listed them as being among officials who overlooked or ignored legal requirements for the abrutply cancelled $149 million bond referendum.

A 14-member jury was chosen on Monday to hear the trial, which is expected to last two or three weeks. Campbell testified Monday and was scheduled to return to the witness stand for cross-examination on Tuesday.
Sales and Clement sought unspecified compensatory damages and attorney fees.
Campbell halted the bond referendum a week before the scheduled vote, mainly because it called for bond maturities of up to 35 years. Georgia law limits public debt amortization to 30 years.
Attorney Mark Trigg, who represents Sales, said the plaintiffs bore no responsibility whatever for the 35 year amortization error.
Canfield said the newspaper accurately reported that they were involved in the bond process.

When Campbell announced on March 8, 1994 that the referendum had been cancelled, former City Finance Officer Michael Bell stepped forward and said he was to blame for the legal oversights. Campbell then accepted all responsibility.
